transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, it's... it's a lot, honestly. I’m an industrial production manager, and for a while there, I was just... I mean, I was on fire. I came in because I went from launching these nonstop, massive plant redesign projects—like, totally overhauling the floor layout to optimize workflow, which is something we’ve needed for years but nobody had the guts to tackle—and I was just doing it. I was calling suppliers after hours, sometimes at like 9 or 10 PM, trying to negotiate bulk rates on new conveyor belts and safety gear, just totally in the zone. I even rewrote the entire shift plan for all three rotations by myself over a weekend. I thought I was just having this incredible streak of productivity, you know? Like everything was finally clicking and I could see exactly how to fix every inefficiency in the plant. But then... it just stopped. And now I’m suddenly completely unable to keep up with the very plans I had set in motion. The redesign is half-finished, the suppliers are calling me back and I can't even pick up the phone, and looking at that shift schedule I made just makes me want to cry because I don't have the energy to even explain it to the floor supervisors. It’s like I built this massive machine and now I’m just getting crushed underneath it, and I don't understand how I went from running the whole show to... this.
Did you feel abnormally happy or on top of the world during that period when you were extremely productive?

Yeah, I mean, at the very beginning of this whole assignment—the redesign project, I mean—I felt... God, "happy" almost doesn't even really cover it. I felt almost electrically upbeat, you know? Like there was this actual, physical current running through my veins and I was just completely dialed into everything. I remember walking onto the factory floor that first week and just grinning at the machinery, feeling like I held the keys to the entire operation and it was all going to be flawless. I was just buzzing with it. 

But then... it didn't stay just happy. It morphed into this weird, intense irritability. Because I had this crystal-clear vision of how the workflow had to go, and whenever anyone—like the senior engineers or the safety inspectors, or even my own boss—whenever they would ask a question or hesitate, I would just lose my patience completely. I felt like anyone questioning my ideas was just dragging their feet and slowing down something that was so incredibly obvious and important. I remember getting into this massive, completely unnecessary argument with the head of procurement because he wanted a couple of days to review the specs I sent him, and I just couldn't fathom why he couldn't see that every hour we waited was a waste. It was like I was sprinting and everyone else was just strolling, and their questions just felt like these deliberate roadblocks to my genius plan, which I know sounds terrible now, but at the time I was just so profoundly annoyed with everyone around me.
Are you currently feeling sad or empty most of the day?

Yeah. Yeah, I am. It's... it's really bad right now. I've been staying in this temporary apartment—my company puts us up in these furnished places when we're overseeing major transitions at different plants, which is usually fine, usually I don't even notice the place because I'm just sleeping there. But lately... lately I wake up in that apartment and it's just this incredibly heavy, hollow feeling right in the center of my chest. Like, the second I open my eyes, before I've even swung my legs out of bed or looked at my phone, I just feel like the entire day is already ruined. It's this profound emptiness, you know? And I just lie there looking at the ceiling, dreading the drive to the plant. I used to use that drive to listen to industry podcasts and mentally map out my meetings, but now it's just... silence. I just sit in the car feeling completely drained and sad, and it doesn't lift. It just sits there with me all day long, no matter what I'm doing or who I'm talking to on the floor. It's like someone just pulled the plug on everything that made me, me, and left this empty shell that just has to somehow keep showing up to work.
Do you feel guilty about how you treated others, like the head of procurement, during your period of high productivity and irritability?

Guilty? I... honestly, no. I mean, I know I probably *should* feel guilty, right? Like, socially, professionally, you're not supposed to bite someone's head off over an email about conveyor belt specs. And Dave—that's the head of procurement, Dave—he's been with the company for like fifteen years, he's a nice guy, he brings donuts on Fridays when we're at the main office, he has pictures of his golden retrievers all over his desk. But... I don't know, even now, looking back at it from this... this heavy, dark place I'm in, I don't actually feel remorse about the argument itself. 

Because the math was right. The workflow was right. I still know, factually, that waiting those two days cost us thousands of dollars in downtime and threw off the installation schedule for the automated sorters. I had the spreadsheets to prove it, I had color-coded the whole timeline. So when I think about yelling at him, I don't get that pit in my stomach like, 'oh, I was so mean.' I just feel... nothing. Or maybe just exhausted by the memory of caring that much. 

It's weird, because usually I'm a very collaborative manager. I pride myself on that, you know? I took all these leadership seminars in grad school about 'synergy' and 'active listening' and I usually try to really implement that on the floor, making sure everyone feels heard and valued. But with Dave, and with the safety inspectors, and everyone else I snapped at during that stretch, I just... I don't have the energy to feel bad about it now. I'm just so drained. My brain is too heavy to even process guilt. It's like my emotional bandwidth is completely maxed out just trying to breathe and get out of bed in that awful apartment. Does that make me a terrible person? I just... I can't even muster up the thought of writing an apology email. I open my laptop and look at his name in my inbox and I just feel completely blank.
Are there things you used to enjoy doing that you no longer find pleasure in?

No, I... I can't really think of anything like that. I mean, I guess I'm not doing much of anything outside of work right now, just because I'm so incredibly exhausted all the time, but it's not like there's some specific hobby I've suddenly lost interest in. I've never really been one of those people with a ton of passionate extracurriculars, you know? My work has always been my main focus. I mean, I played volleyball in high school and a little bit in undergrad, just intramural stuff, but I haven't touched a ball in years, so that doesn't count. And I used to read a lot—mostly historical non-fiction, biographies of industrial pioneers, that kind of thing—but honestly, I haven't had the time or the mental energy to read a whole book since I started this job three years ago. 

So it's not like I have this vibrant social life or these deep passions that I'm suddenly neglecting. Usually, my idea of a good weekend is just catching up on sleep, maybe going for a run if the weather's nice, and getting a head start on my emails for Monday. And I guess I'm not running right now, but that's just because I feel so heavy and drained, not because I don't *want* to enjoy it. It's just hard to care about anything when you feel this empty. But as far as, like, specific things I used to love doing that I just don't care about anymore? No, I don't think so. I'm just... I'm just existing right now. Just trying to get through the day at the plant and then get back to that apartment so I can lie down again.
Do you feel like you're a failure now compared to how you felt during your period of high productivity?

Failure? I... no, I wouldn't use that word. I don't feel like a failure, exactly. I mean, I know what failure looks like in my field. Failure is when a production line goes down for 48 hours because someone didn't order the right replacement bearings, or when a safety inspection results in a massive fine. I haven't done that. I'm still showing up. I'm still doing my job, even though it feels like I'm moving through wet concrete just to get from my car to my desk.

It's more like... it's like a profound sense of loss, maybe? Because during that stretch a few months ago, when I was completely redesigning the workflow for the packing department in a single weekend, I felt so incredibly capable. I felt like I was firing on all cylinders, like my brain was a supercomputer and everyone else was just using abacuses. I was making connections between the supply chain and the floor schedule that the senior directors hadn't even noticed. I felt powerful. I felt like I was exactly where I was supposed to be, doing exactly what I was meant to do, and nothing could slow me down. I didn't even need sleep to do it.

And now... now I'm just this heavy, slow version of myself. I look at the same spreadsheets that used to make perfect sense to me, the ones where I could instantly spot the inefficiencies, and now it just looks like a wall of meaningless numbers. It takes me an hour just to draft a simple email to the shift supervisors because I can't find the words. I just stare at the screen and feel this crushing weight in my chest. So, I guess I don't feel like a failure, because I know I have the capacity to be brilliant—I *was* brilliant, just a little while ago. But I feel completely disconnected from that person. I feel like that version of me is gone, and I'm just stuck here, in this awful apartment, in this exhausted body, wondering if I'll ever get my brain back. It's not failure, it's just... it's just so incredibly sad to know how good I can be, and to feel so completely incapable of being that person right now.
Have you had any thoughts of not wanting to be alive or wishing you could just disappear?

No, I... I haven't really thought about dying. I mean, not in the sense of actually wanting to end my life or, you know, making any sort of plan. I know that's a thing people worry about when you get this low, but that's not really where my head is at. I don't want to die. I just... 

I guess "disappear" is a strong word, but I do have this overwhelming desire to just... pause everything. You know? Like, if I could just hit a massive pause button on the entire world, on the plant, on the supply chain, on the emails from Dave in procurement, on the rent being due for this terrible apartment where the radiator clanks all night... if I could just stop all of it for a month, maybe two, and just sleep. Just lie in a dark, quiet room where nobody needs anything from me and I don't have to make any decisions or look at any spreadsheets. 

It's not about not being alive, it's just about the sheer exhaustion of *being*. The effort it takes to maintain my existence right now is just staggering. Waking up, making coffee I don't even want to drink, putting on clothes, driving to the plant, pretending I'm still the competent manager I was three months ago... it's like I'm dragging a hundred-pound weight behind me every single second of the day. So, when I'm lying in bed at night, staring at the ceiling and listening to the traffic outside, I don't think "I wish I were dead." I think, "I wish I could just dissolve into the mattress and not have to do tomorrow." I just want a break from the heaviness of my own brain. But no, no actual thoughts of, like, self-harm or suicide or anything like that. Just this deep, deep craving for everything to stop demanding things from me.
Did you ever feel like you didn't need sleep during those highly productive periods?

Oh, absolutely. It was the strangest thing, honestly. Normally, I'm someone who needs a solid seven or eight hours, or at least I try to get that, even if I'm just lying there thinking about the production schedule. But during that time... it was like sleep just became this completely irrelevant concept. I remember it so clearly because it started on a Tuesday, which is usually our heaviest day for inbound freight, and I stayed up almost the entire night drafting that new workflow I mentioned earlier. I think I finally laid down around 4:00 AM, and my alarm went off at 6:00 AM. 

And the crazy part is, when that alarm went off, I didn't feel groggy at all. Not even a little bit. I popped right out of bed. I felt completely refreshed, like I'd slept for ten hours. I was sleeping maybe two or three hours a night for weeks, and I was still showing up at the plant feeling completely sharp and charged. It was like I had this internal battery that was just constantly regenerating itself without me having to do anything. I actually remember thinking that sleep was just optional, you know? Like it was this incredibly inefficient biological flaw that I had somehow managed to evolve past. I even started getting annoyed at my coworkers who would complain about being tired after working a ten-hour shift, because I was doing fourteen-hour days, going home, working on my laptop until 3:00 AM, and then doing it all over again without even a yawn. It felt amazing at the time, like I had unlocked this secret extra portion of the day that nobody else had access to. But now... now I just feel like I'm paying the debt for all those missed hours of sleep, with interest. It's like my body is trying to claw back every single minute I didn't sleep back then.
Did you spend more money than usual during that highly productive period

Money? No, actually, I don't think I did. In fact, I'm pretty sure I spent less than usual during that whole stretch. Because, I mean, if you think about it, when would I have even had the time to spend money? I was at the plant for fourteen, sometimes fifteen hours a day. And when I wasn't physically in the office or on the floor, I was sitting at my kitchen island—which, by the way, is this really cheap faux-granite thing the landlord installed right before I moved in, the laminate is actually peeling on the corner where I sit—but I'd be sitting there with my laptop open until three in the morning, completely engrossed in the packing department's shift rotations and the inbound freight logs. 

I wasn't browsing online or going to stores. I just didn't care about any of that. The concept of buying things just seemed so... trivial, I guess? Like, why would I waste my time looking at clothes or gadgets when I was in the middle of revolutionizing our entire supply chain protocol? The only things I was really buying were gas to get back and forth to the plant, and maybe coffee. Though, honestly, I was so wired and focused that I usually didn't even bother stopping at the drive-thru. I just drank the terrible, burnt coffee from the breakroom because it was closer to my desk and I didn't want to break my concentration. 

I know some people go out and buy cars or max out their credit cards when they get really, really energized like that. My sister actually asked me about it at one point, because I called her on a Sunday morning and I was talking so fast about my workflow redesign that she asked if I was out on some kind of shopping spree. But no, money just wasn't on my radar at all. It was entirely about efficiency. The plant's efficiency, my own efficiency. Spending money takes time—you have to look at things, compare them, input your card details—and all my processing power was strictly allocated to the floor schedule. 

I think literally the most extravagant thing I bought during those entire three or four weeks was a new pack of dry-erase markers and some very specific highlighters from the office supply store down the street. I needed them because I was color-coding the inbound freight versus the outbound shipments on my master board, and the ones we had in the supply closet at work were the wrong shades of green and blue, and I needed the visual distinction to be absolutely perfect so I could read it from across the room. So, yeah, I spent maybe twelve dollars on office supplies. My bank account actually looked great because I wasn't going out to eat or doing anything social. Now, of course, I'm not spending money either, but that's just because the thought of even opening a food delivery app and having to choose what to eat makes me want to cry. But back then, no, no wild spending at all. Just the highlighters.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight recently?

Weight... well, I don't actually own a scale. Or, wait, I think I have one but it's shoved way under the bathroom sink behind a bunch of cleaning supplies I haven't used in months. But I can tell my clothes are fitting weird, mostly because my eating is just... it's completely all over the place right now. It's total chaos. 

Like, some days I'll be sitting at my desk at the plant, just staring at my inbox and feeling like I can barely keep my head up, and suddenly I'll look at the clock and it's 4:00 p.m. and I realize that literally all I've had all day is coffee. Just that same awful, burnt breakroom coffee I mentioned before. I don't even feel my stomach rumble. It's like my body just forgets that it needs fuel, or maybe it just knows I don't have the energy to chew anything anyway. The thought of eating just feels like another massive chore on a list of chores I'm already failing at.

But then, it's so weird, because on the flip side, other nights I'll finally drag myself home, and I'll order delivery because the thought of actually cooking or even opening the refrigerator is just overwhelmingly exhausting. And when the food gets there, I don't even sit down at that peeling kitchen island. I don't get a plate or a napkin. I literally just stand there in the middle of the kitchen, under this really harsh fluorescent light that always gives me a headache, eating takeout straight from the plastic container. And the crazy thing is, I'm not even really hungry when I'm doing it. I'm just standing there eating cold noodles mechanically, almost like I'm just trying to fill up some empty space inside me, even though food doesn't actually fix it. 

So I have no idea what my actual weight is doing numerically, but with the way I'm either accidentally fasting all day or standing around eating heavy takeout at night without even wanting it... my body just doesn't know what to do with itself right now.
Are there any activities, either related to work or in your personal life, that you used to find enjoyable but no longer do?

Enjoyable activities... gosh, I mean, right now, the concept of enjoyment just feels completely foreign. It's like I'm looking at everything through this thick pane of frosted glass, you know? Like I can see that things are happening, but I can't actually connect with them or feel anything about them. 

Take my job, for instance. I'm an industrial production manager, and honestly, I used to love it. I used to thrive on it. Even before that whole crazy productive period I told you about, I always enjoyed the puzzle of it all. Figuring out how to optimize the floor, making sure the inbound freight synced up perfectly with the outbound shipments, troubleshooting when a machine went down... it used to give me this real sense of satisfaction. I'd go home feeling like I actually accomplished something tangible. But now? Now I pull into the parking lot at the plant and I just sit in my car for twenty minutes, staring at the steering wheel, dreading having to walk through those doors. The floor schedule, the freight logs, the shift rotations... it's all just this massive, gray mountain of obligation that I can't even begin to scale. It's not just that I don't enjoy it anymore; it's that the thought of doing it actually makes me feel physically heavy, like my limbs are made of lead.

And it's not just work, either. It's everything. I used to love reading. I have this whole bookshelf in my living room, mostly historical fiction and some biographies, and I used to tear through a book a week. I loved getting lost in a different time period or someone else's life. It was my way of decompressing. But I haven't picked up a book in... I don't even know how long. A couple of months, maybe? I tried a few weeks ago. I grabbed this new novel I'd bought back when I still cared about things, and I sat on the couch, and I read the same paragraph over and over again for maybe ten minutes. The words just wouldn't stick in my brain. They were just shapes on a page. I couldn't picture the characters, I didn't care what happened to them, and I just ended up putting the book face down on the coffee table and staring at the wall instead. 

Even little things, like... I used to really like making coffee on Sunday mornings. I have this French press, and I'd buy these nice, locally roasted beans, and the whole ritual of grinding them and pouring the water and smelling it... it was this nice, quiet moment I had to myself before the week started. Now, like I said, I just drink whatever burnt sludge is in the breakroom, or I don't drink anything at all. The thought of getting the French press out of the cupboard, cleaning it, boiling the water... it's just exhausting. Everything is exhausting. There's just no joy left in any of it. It's all just... maintenance. Just trying to get through the day without completely falling apart, and even that feels like it's taking everything I have.
Do you feel less confident in your abilities now compared to before this period of low productivity?

Less confident? God, yes. I mean, right now, I don't even trust myself to send a basic email without second-guessing every single word. I feel completely incompetent, like I'm just an imposter taking up space in my own office and everyone is about to figure out that I actually have no idea what I'm doing. 

But before this? Back during that really energized stretch I was telling you about? It was the exact opposite. It's almost embarrassing to think about now, because the contrast is just so extreme. Back then, we actually had this external consulting team come in—corporate hired them for, I don't even want to know how much money, these guys in expensive suits with their endless, completely useless PowerPoint decks, trying to tell us how to optimize the floor schedule. And I just sat in on one of their meetings and I honestly believed, with every fiber of my being, that I could fix the entire production workflow faster than that whole consulting team combined. 

I was absolutely certain of it. I looked at their projections and I just thought, "This is amateur hour, these guys are moving in slow motion." I literally went back to my desk, or, well, my peeling kitchen island at three in the morning, and started completely overhauling the routing protocols myself. My supervisor actually tried to pull me aside at one point. He had some serious reservations about me changing the inbound freight logs so drastically without running a beta test first, but I just completely brushed off his concerns. I basically waved him away. I didn't want to hear it, because in my head, failure didn't even seem possible to me. It wasn't even a concept I could grasp. 

I was so sure that my brain was operating on this entirely different, elevated plane, and I was the only one who could see how all the pieces of the plant fit together. I felt completely bulletproof. I thought I was a genius, honestly. And now... I mean, now I look at those exact same workflow charts I made and I can't even make sense of them. The drop-off is just... it's really hard to reconcile that I'm the same person who was practically laughing at those consultants a few months ago, when today I can't even figure out how to get through a single shift without wanting to hide under my desk.
Do you feel worthless or have a significantly lowered opinion of yourself now compared to before this period of low productivity?

Worthless? Um... no, I don't think I would use that word. I mean, I know I just went on and on about feeling incompetent at the plant right now and second-guessing every single word of my emails, but that's... I feel like that's different than feeling worthless as a human being, if that makes sense? 

Like, logically, I know I have value. I have a graduate degree, and I worked incredibly hard for that. I spent years sitting in seminars, writing massive case studies on supply chain logistics, and pulling all-nighters to get to where I am in my career. So I know, deep down, that I'm an educated, capable person. I don't think I'm a waste of space in the grand scheme of things. It's more just that my current... my execution is completely broken right now. 

So when I'm sitting there at my desk, staring blankly at the screen and failing to do something simple, I'm not thinking, "Oh, I have no worth, I'm a terrible person." It's more like, "Why won't my brain just do the thing it's supposed to do?" It feels like a mechanical failure, you know? Like a machine breaking down on the floor, rather than a moral failing or a complete lack of human worth. 

And as for having a lowered opinion of myself... I mean, obviously, I don't think I'm the untouchable, visionary genius I thought I was back when I was trying to rewrite all the inbound freight protocols and laughing at those expensive corporate consultants. That was... well, that was obviously a very inflated version of myself. But my actual baseline opinion of who I am hasn't really crashed into the basement. Honestly, I'm just so unbelievably tired that I don't even have the mental bandwidth to sit around philosophizing about my self-worth. I'm just trying to survive the shift. I'm not sitting in my car in the parking lot dreading work because I hate myself, I'm dreading it because the actual physical and mental tasks just feel completely impossible to get through. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel worthless at all. Just... really, really stuck.
Have you noticed any changes in your sex drive recently?

Sex drive? Um... no, I haven't really noticed any changes there, actually. Which, now that you ask, I guess might sound a little strange considering how completely upended the rest of my life feels right now, with the exhaustion and the brain fog I was just telling you about. But yeah, no, it's pretty much stayed exactly the same. Just... baseline, I guess? 

I'm not currently seeing anyone, and I haven't been dating seriously for a couple of years now, mostly because being a production manager means my schedule is completely unpredictable. When you're managing a floor that runs three shifts and you're the one getting called at two in the morning because a conveyor belt jammed or a freight delivery got delayed, dating just sort of falls off the radar. So sex just hasn't been a major focus for me in general for a long time. 

Even back a few months ago during that really energized stretch where I was staying up all night completely overhauling the routing protocols and feeling like I could conquer the world, my sex drive didn't suddenly spike or anything. I wasn't going out to bars or looking for hookups or suddenly feeling hyper-sexual. I was just entirely fixated on the plant and the workflow. And now, even with everything feeling so incredibly heavy and impossible to get through, that specific part of me hasn't really dropped off either. It's just... neutral. Like it always is. I just haven't noticed any difference at all. So, no, no changes there, up or down. It's probably the one single thing in my life right now that actually hasn't fluctuated.
Do you find it harder to concentrate or make decisions now compared to before you started feeling this way?

Oh, god, yes. It’s... honestly, it’s probably the most frightening part of all of this right now. My brain just feels like it’s wading through wet cement. 

Just to give you a really specific example of how bad it’s gotten—we had our weekly shift-planning meeting a few days ago. And usually, this is my bread and butter, right? I actually designed the color-coded Excel matrix we use for these meetings. I usually sit at the head of the conference table in the glass room overlooking the floor, and I just rapid-fire the allocations. I can usually juggle who is on PTO, who is cross-trained on the stamping machines, what the maintenance windows are, all of it, without even really needing to look at my notes. 

But this time... I was looking up at the projector, looking at the staffing numbers on the screen, and I just... I couldn’t hold them in my head. At all. I would look at the headcount for the loading dock, and by the time my eyes moved over to the forklift operators column, the first number was just completely gone. Wiped from my memory. And my floor supervisors were all just sitting there, drinking their coffee, staring at me, waiting for me to make a basic decision about weekend overtime allocations. Just a simple, routine decision on whether we needed to hold over three guys from the second shift to meet a quota. 

And I couldn't do it. I couldn't hold the staffing numbers in my head long enough to make a basic decision. I just sat there staring at the cells on the spreadsheet like they were written in ancient Greek. I couldn't synthesize the information to make a choice. It is genuinely terrifying, to be honest with you, because that is normally exactly my job. That is what they pay me to do, it's what I went to grad school for, to look at that exact kind of logistical data and make the call. 

I ended up having to pretend I was choking on my water just so I could excuse myself and go stand in the bathroom, because I was so panicked that they were going to realize my brain is just completely empty right now. Before all this, like I said, I could juggle a dozen variables at once while answering an email and talking to a vendor. Now, I can't even hold two numbers in my head for five seconds to make a call on basic staffing. It’s like the RAM in my brain is completely fried. I just sit there paralyzed.
Do you feel like you're less capable or less intelligent than you used to be?

Less intelligent? Um... no. No, I wouldn't say that. It’s actually kind of tied to what I was saying earlier about not feeling worthless, you know? I know the intelligence is still in there somewhere. I didn't just suddenly lose my IQ points or forget everything I spent years learning in grad school. 

Let me put it this way, because I think about this a lot when I'm sitting at my desk trying to force myself to work. On the production floor, we have these massive, multi-million dollar CNC stamping presses. They are incredibly sophisticated, highly programmed pieces of equipment. They can execute these flawless, microscopic tolerances on heavy steel. But if there's a drop in the pneumatic pressure, or if a tiny safety sensor gets covered in a layer of factory dust, the machine just halts. It completely stops working. It won't even punch a single hole. But that doesn't mean the machine suddenly became a cheap, useless piece of junk, right? The programming is all still in there. The actual inherent capability of the machine hasn't changed at all. It's just... the system is jammed and won't execute.

That's exactly how I feel about my brain right now. I don't feel like I've actually *become* a less intelligent person. I know I'm smart. I know I'm capable of running that plant, and I know I understand complex supply chain logistics better than almost anyone else in that building. But the pneumatic pressure in my head is just gone. The system is halted. So when I'm sitting there and I can't do a basic shift-planning matrix, it's not because I'm suddenly too dumb to understand basic addition and subtraction. It's because the machinery of my brain is just... refusing to run the program. 

And honestly, that almost makes it worse. It's incredibly frustrating because I *know* I'm capable. If I actually thought I was just losing my intelligence, if I thought I was just naturally not smart enough to do the job anymore, maybe I'd just accept it and step down or find an easier career. But I know the knowledge is in there. I can almost feel the information trapped behind this huge, heavy wall of fog and exhaustion. I just sit there staring at my monitor and I think, "Come on, you know this, you've done this a thousand times," but the connection just won't complete. 

So, no, I definitely don't feel less intelligent or inherently less capable. I know who I am and what I can do when I'm actually functioning. I just feel... mechanically broken at the moment, if that makes sense.
Have you found yourself less able to come up with creative solutions to problems at work or in your personal life lately?

Well, yeah, I mean... it really goes right back to what I was just telling you a minute ago about that shift-planning meeting. Because usually, coming up with creative solutions is the best part of my day. If we have a bottleneck on the floor, I don't just look at the schedule and force mandatory overtime. I get creative with it. I’ll look at the cross-training matrix, figure out if we can pull a guy from shipping who knows how to run the secondary stamping press, stagger the maintenance windows, maybe reroute a freight delivery to dock four instead of dock one so we don't have a forklift traffic jam... it's like a giant puzzle, and I'm usually really good at finding those out-of-the-box workarounds. 

But lately? No. Not at all. Because, exactly like I just said about that meeting, I couldn't even hold the basic staffing numbers in my head long enough to make a simple, routine decision, let alone a creative one. You can't think outside the box when you can't even remember what's *in* the box, you know? 

And it is just so terrifying to me, because that kind of dynamic problem-solving is normally exactly my job. It's what I'm known for at the plant. If a conveyor belt goes down, my regional director doesn't want me to just sit there and say, 'Oh well, we lose a day of production.' They want me to figure out a clever way to bypass it, to keep the quota moving. But right now, if you asked me to do that, I couldn't. I'd just stare at you. Because to be creative, to find those unique solutions, you have to be able to hold multiple variables in your head at the same time and play with them, turn them around, see how they fit together. And I... I just can't do that right now. Like I said, the numbers just vanish the second I look away from the spreadsheet. So the creativity is just completely gone, because the basic mental machinery required to even process the raw information just isn't functioning.
